BACONC PILIP'NAS Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA cor. Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City www.dilq.qov.ph s. 2021 on-G OPINION NO JUL 032024 GEORGE KARLOS SUSTENTO Sustento.geo@gmail.com Dear Mr. Sustento: This is in reference to your electronic mail dated January 27, 2024, seeking clarification on the definition of a public servant and public official. Specifically, you inquired whether officials and employees of Electric Cooperatives would fall under these categories. You referenced the Administrative Code of 1987, which defines "public official" or "public servant" as any government employee who holds some level of authority to act on behalf of the government and in the interest of the public. The Code also defines "employees" as individuals serving the government or any of its agencies, divisions, subdivisions, or instrumentalities. Expanding on your inquiry, you pose the question of whether the nature of Electric Cooperatives, which essentially exist to serve the interests of their members—who are also consumers—and receive government subsidies, qualifies their officials and employees as public servants. Notably, you cited Republic Act No. 11659, which designates electric distributors as a public service. Hence, your query: "Given that Electric Cooperatives are a public service and they depend in part on the people's tax through subsidies as well as their ownership being by the community and its members, should we also expect them to follow the standards we have set for those that are direct employees of the govemment?" Foremost, we find it imperative to delineate the concept of a public servant. Notably, the Administrative Code of 1987 (Executive Order No. 292) did not specifically define the term "public servant" or "public officer." A closer scrutiny of the Administrative Code, however, would reveal the nuanced characteristics of an "officer," distinguishing it from an "employee." Section 2 thereof reads: "Officer" as distinguished from "clerk" or "employee", refers to a person whose duties, not being of a clerical or manual nature, involves the exercise of discretion in the performance of the functions of the government. When used with reference to a person having authority to do a particular act or perform a particular function in the exercise of governmental power, "officer" includes any government employee, agent or body having authority to do the act or exercise that function." "Employee", when used with reference to a person in the public service, includes any person in the service of the government or any of its agencies, divisions, subdivisions or instrumentalities." "Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

Pertinently, Republic Act No. 6713, otherwise known as the "Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees," provides a comprehensive definition as to what constitutes "public servant" or "public official." In particular, Section 3 thereof reads, "Public officials include elective and appointive officials and employees, permanent or temporary, whether in the career or non-career service, including military and police personnel, whether or not they receive compensation, regardless of amount. " We also find it equally imperative to delineate the nature of cooperatives, such as electric cooperatives. By their inherent function, cooperatives exist to serve the interests of their members—who are also consumers—and often receive subsidies from the government. Along this line, it is well to note that generally, cooperatives have by-laws, which fundamentally govern the conduct of their officials and members. Such by-laws generally define the parameters, functions, and decision-making processes, among other things related to the operation and dynamics of cooperatives. Interestingly, you underscore that Republic Act No. 11659 designates electric distributors, including Electric Cooperatives, as entities providing public service. Premised from the foregoing, we are of the opinion that the barometer determination of whether Electric Cooperatives' officials and employees qualify as public servants hinges fundamentally on the nature and extent of their authority, functions, and relationship to the government. It is important to note that while Electric Cooperatives are generally privately owned and operated; hence, albeit playing a vital role in delivering essential utilities to communities, the employees thereof are privately employed and are not considered public employees or public officials. It is the whole electric cooperative, as an entity, which serves an important public service function as a franchisee of a public utility. We cite P.D. No. 269 s. 1973 which provided a definition of cooperatives and public service entities as used in the concept of National Electrification Administration (NEA), to wit: (b) "Cooperative" shall mean a corporation organized under Republic Act No. 6038 or this Decree or cooperative supplying or empowered to supply service which has heretofore been organized under the Philippine NonAgricuItural Cooperative Act, whether covered under this Decree or not. (c) "Public service entities" shall mean (I) a cooperative, (2) the NPC, and (3) local governments and privately-owned public service entities in operation which furnish and are empowered to furnish retail electric service. Notwithstanding, this opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities or the courts. We hope to have guided you accordingly.
